tracks.title: Who is awake at 3am?
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 4 — keepers. A sub-lesson, under the nexus. The nexus lesson made a promise — a docked workbook is stateful… schedules fire overnight, the work keeps moving while the page is closed. [curious] Lovely sentence. It's also the exact sentence every agent demo breaks. The terminal closes, the session ends, the context window evaporates — and the always-on agent turns out to be a person holding a laptop open. So this is the honest version of that promise. Something has to be awake at three in the morning, and it has to be a real process you can name. The fair questions are blunt. First… what process is ticking? Second… what decides what it does on each tick? And third… what happens when it crashes, hangs forever, or wakes up to find nothing to do? A scheduler that can't answer the third question isn't a scheduler — it's a hope. The answer is a keeper. And the satisfying part is how boring it turns out to be. No platform, no daemon mesh — one supervised worker, a timer message, a wall-clock bound, and a text file holding the last-run timestamp. About four hundred lines.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A keeper is a supervised worker that ticks an agent definition on a cadence — entirely on-box. One per agent. The runtime owns when… the def owns what. A keeper belongs entirely to the host layer. It reads a loaded artifact — your agent def — but it never touches the public plane and never crosses the Dock membrane. And when it runs the agent, it goes through the exact same path as an interactive request you typed. A scheduled run and a typed request are the same code… only the trigger differs. There's a trinity of names worth fixing now. First… the worker — the tick engine, one per agent. Second… the keeper — a singleton facade that starts exactly one worker, for a single standing agent. Third… the crew — a supervisor that starts one worker per agent from a manifest. The singleton is just a crew of one.

tracks.title: Anatomy of a tick
tracks.text: Anatomy of a tick. Picture one tick, whole. A timer fires the message tick. The worker wakes, and in order it does six things. First… it writes the current time to its last-run file. Second… optionally, it pulls git — integrating human and CI pushes, if you opted in. Third… it decides what this tick is, a lifecycle step. Fourth… it runs the agent def, in a linked task, with the working directory set to the page's own git repo. Fifth… the run returns one of four outcomes — done, failed, killed, or no-work. And sixth… it schedules the next tick, with a delay chosen by that outcome. Three details make this survivable. One — the run has a wall-clock bound, fifteen minutes by default. If it blows the clock, it's shut down brutally and the outcome is killed. A wedged run can't hang the schedule. Two — the worker traps exits, so a crash inside the run never takes the worker down. Three — every commit the run makes lands in the page's git repo… which means those commits are the public changelog. [chuckles] There's a war story in the code here. Before the tenant was wired correctly, the landing site committed four posts that all returned not-found — they'd published to a build folder instead of the served root. The fix was making the run's working directory the tenant repo… not guessing.

tracks.title: Time that survives restarts
tracks.text: Time that survives restarts. This is the most important fact about a keeper — where its schedule lives. Not in memory. On disk. Each tick writes the current time to a plain text file called keeper-last-run, on the data volume, beside the work. So picture the boot decision as a little flowchart. The worker boots, and asks — does the last-run file exist? If no… the first tick fires after a sixty-second boot-grace floor, not on boot, because booting isn't doing work. If yes… it computes elapsed time since the last run, and sets the delay to the larger of sixty seconds, or the interval minus the elapsed time. So if the full interval already passed while you were down, that same sixty-second floor applies — a flapping deploy can't hammer the model. Otherwise, it fires in the remainder. Here's the whole thing in numbers. A keeper that last ran eleven minutes ago, on a fifteen-minute interval, redeployed right now… ticks in four minutes. Not fifteen. A redeploy never resets the cadence clock. [excited] And there's a second mode — continuous mode — which replaces the full interval with a short breather, forty-five seconds by default, for agents that should loop nearly without rest.

tracks.title: What each tick is
tracks.text: What each tick is — a depth rung, skippable, but it's where a timer becomes an orchestrator. So far each tick was the same — run the def. But the orchestrator agent has a true workflow… a deterministic state machine, declared in native org, executed one transition per tick. The org file owns the spec. The runtime just steps it. Picture the canonical loop, read aloud. It starts at wake-add. Wake-add has kind wake — meaning run the agent — a repeat of three, and a next edge to wake-audit. So… add work, three successful ticks in a row. Then wake-audit — kind wake, next edge to rem. Then rem — kind rem, which means dream, no agent runs at all — with a next edge to wake-plan, and a minimum interval of ten minutes, a time gate. Then wake-plan — kind wake — whose next edge loops back to wake-add. So the whole loop is… add three times, audit once, dream if ten minutes have passed, plan, and back to adding. Position is a pair — state, and hits — and it persists to a file called lifecycle-pos, so a redeploy resumes mid-loop, the file literally reading wake-add two. Now the transition rule, which is the crisp part. On done… hits go up by one, and at the repeat count, take the next edge and reset. On no-work… collapse the remaining repeats and take the edge now — but this is a fast-forward, never a skip. Every state in the declared order still runs, so the audit and the dream keep their cadence. And on failed or killed… hold position, retry the same state next tick. That's the global failure rule — cadence survives crashes. Let me trace six ticks. Tick one — wake-add, zero hits, outcome done, moves to wake-add with one hit. Tick two — wake-add, one hit, outcome failed… stays at wake-add one hit, a retry, cadence held. Tick three — wake-add, one hit, done… moves to two hits. Tick four — wake-add, two hits, outcome no-work… jumps to wake-audit, repeats collapsed but never skipped. Tick five — wake-audit, done… moves to rem. Tick six — rem, but only four minutes since the last dream… so the tick is gated, a no-op, and the position waits. [curious] Read tick two and tick four together. A failure costs you nothing but a retry. And a no-work doesn't let the agent dodge its audit — it just stops grinding adds that have nothing left to add.

tracks.title: The economics of doing nothing
tracks.text: The economics of doing nothing. [curious] Every wake tick is an LLM call, and an LLM call costs real money. So the expensive question isn't what a busy keeper does — it's what an idle one costs. The honest answer used to be… too much. An early crew burned a model call every ten seconds just to report there was nothing to do. Two mechanisms fixed that. First… the no-work protocol. An agent signals an empty tick by beginning its result with the literal word NO-WORK. The worker reads that prefix and records the outcome — no commit, no fuss. Second… exponential idle backoff. Consecutive empty ticks stretch the gap. Picture the streak climbing. One empty tick — wait one minute. Two — two minutes. Three — four. Four — eight. Five — sixteen. Six or more — capped at thirty minutes. And the verdict, in one line… a keeper with nothing to do settles into a thirty-minute heartbeat within six idle ticks — and the moment it finds work, a single done snaps it straight back to full cadence on the very next beat. [excited] Doing nothing should be nearly free. And here it is.

tracks.title: From one keeper to a newsroom
tracks.text: From one keeper to a newsroom. One standing agent is the singleton. Several agents ticking together is a crew — a supervisor that starts one worker per member, from a manifest. And the manifest is plain org. Let me read the real bit.ml newsroom aloud. Heading desk — its def at desk dot org, interval forty-five minutes. Heading moss — the researcher, interval fifteen minutes. Heading wren — the writer, interval fifteen minutes. And heading hale — the editor, interval twenty minutes. Four agents, each on its own clock, each running its own def. The def property is required — a member without it is skipped. The interval accepts durations like fifteen-m, two-h, ninety-s, or bare milliseconds. Two design choices keep a crew sane. First… staggered boots. Worker one fires at zero seconds, worker two at thirty, worker three at sixty, worker four at ninety — they overlap without a thundering herd of model calls at boot. Second… fully namespaced state. Every persistence file is per-agent — last-run-wren, lifecycle-pos-wren — so the agents tick independently with no shared clock. And the two modes are mutually exclusive — a crew manifest wins, then a single def, then neither child exists at all. The singleton and the crew differ in one comparison worth saying plainly… the singleton runs one worker with no concurrency gate, while the crew runs one worker per agent behind a shared gate that caps how many run at once.

tracks.title: The gate and the claim
tracks.text: The gate and the claim — another depth rung. Four agents on fifteen-minute intervals will sometimes wake at once, and four simultaneous LLM runs is a way to set money on fire. So a crew shares one global concurrency cap — a counting semaphore, default two runs at a time. Picture three agents and two slots. Moss acquires slot one. Wren acquires slot two. Hale tries to acquire… and parks — it joins a first-in-first-out queue and waits, with no timeout, so it can never starve. Then moss finishes and releases its slot… and the gate hands that slot directly to the head of the queue — hale — which now runs. The release happens in an after block, so even a crashed or timed-out run always returns its slot. Capacity can't leak. Now the sharp line. You might expect the runtime to lock a task so two agents can't grab the same one. It doesn't. Board claims are a def-level protocol, not a runtime lock. An agent claims work by flipping a task to doing and committing an agent property to git — with its own name on it — before it starts. That commit is visible to every peer, in git, before any work happens. The runtime's job is narrower and honest — it isolates runs and throttles concurrency. Coordination is the agents' protocol, played out in the open.

tracks.title: Watching it work
tracks.text: Watching it work. A process awake at three a.m. is only trustworthy if you can see it. The public plane exposes two read-only endpoints. The changes endpoint returns the recent git log plus the keeper's status — the commits the keeper made are the changelog. The activity endpoint returns live telemetry — for a crew, a per-agent breakdown plus a merged wire of recent steps, each tagged with the agent that emitted it. Picture that crew shape as a small object. There's an agents list — and one entry might be… name wren, running true, lifecycle in state wake-add at one hit, its last five steps, and its current thought. Then a wire array — recent steps across everyone, each tagged with its agent. And a legacy block naming the single busiest agent, for older frontends. And here's a detail that matters more than it looks — status is published to a lock-free shared term and read from there, never by calling the worker. Why? Because a tick runs synchronously inside the worker — a status call would block for the whole run, up to fifteen minutes. Reading the published term means the dashboard is instant even while the agent is mid-thought. You can also nudge a keeper by hand — run-once sends a single tick immediately. And the living landing site is the proof. Its keeper — Waldo, the Workbook Autonomous Live Document Operator — runs every fifteen minutes, the fourth run each hour being the audit pass, every commit appearing in the page's timeline. [excited] The schedule is real, the agent is real, and you can watch it from a browser.

tracks.title: Schedules in the source
tracks.text: Schedules in the source. There are several places declared time lives in this ecosystem, and it's worth being precise about which one actually ticks. A workflow headline can carry a schedule property or a native scheduled timestamp — and the kernel surfaces that as a schedule field, which the plan endpoint reports without executing anything. A crew member declares its cadence with an interval property. A lifecycle state declares a time gate with a minimum-interval property. Now the honest framing, because it's easy to blur. Nothing in the host cron-executes a workflow's schedule on its own — that field is declared, surfaced metadata. Plan output and run records. The thing that actually wakes up and runs on a clock is the keeper — its interval, its lifecycle, its gates. The workflow schedule is what a keeper's agent reads and acts on. The keeper is the engine that does the waking. So don't picture a built-in cron daemon firing schedule lines — picture a keeper ticking, and an agent inside it consulting the plan.

tracks.title: What keepers aren't
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what keepers aren't. A keeper is an interval-and-lifecycle ticker, and it's sharpest when you know its edges. First… it is not a cron engine for workflow schedules. A schedule on a workflow is surfaced metadata today, not an autonomous trigger — the keeper's own interval is the live clock. Second… it is not a task-lock service. Two agents avoid the same task through a def-level protocol committed to git — a visible claim made before the work — not a runtime mutex. Third… it is not free. Every wake tick is a model call with a real bill, which is the whole reason the no-work protocol and the backoff exist. The economics are designed in. And fourth… it is not transactional. The fifteen-minute wall-clock kill is genuinely brutal — a wedged run is shut down hard, mid-work. [sighs] There's no rollback. A half-finished run is recovered the honest way — by git, and a retry of the same state next tick. The cadence survives the crash. The partial work is abandoned and redone.

tracks.title: Back up to the nexus
tracks.text: So that's a keeper. The process that's awake at three a.m. — and it's boring on purpose. One supervised worker, a timer, a wall-clock bound, and a few text files holding the schedule on disk so a redeploy resumes mid-loop. The runtime owns when… the def owns what. [curious] If the process model felt new, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under the nexus — lesson 02 — the engine whose stateful promise this whole page keeps. Go there for the supervision tree and the isolation model. And the agent it ticks has its own lesson too — lesson five — the worker with tenure. Everything a keeper does… is built from those two.
